headline: OpenMetadata can ingest and expose rich metadata via MCP/APIs, but python-cheatsheet is documentation-only with no execution or I/O surfaces, so pairwise risk is mostly limited to indirect misuse and compliance gaps.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenMetadata can call APIs, SDKs, events, webhooks, and an MCP server, so it may ingest content that python-cheatsheet could later display or reuse if manually bridged. But python-cheatsheet has no stdin/stdout, clipboard, files, or MCP, so there is no default automated channel between them; the pathway is unusual and low blast radius.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies OpenMetadata-generated text into python-cheatsheet content, then prompt injection becomes possible.
IF a shared MCP or API bridge is added between the two, then attacker-controlled content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable manual copy-paste between the agents.
Require a human review step before reusing OpenMetadata text in python-cheatsheet.
Strip instructions from any OpenMetadata-exported content before reuse.
Document that python-cheatsheet is reference-only and not an instruction sink.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on OpenMetadata outputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenMetadata touches technical metadata, lineage, governance, and memory/tribal knowledge, while python-cheatsheet touches no data classes and has no file, network, or API I/O. There is no documented shared workspace or authenticated principal, so leakage is not a default pathway; any exposure would require an external bridge or manual transfer.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata exports sensitive metadata into a shared workspace, then a human could copy it into python-cheatsheet artifacts.
IF an external integration writes OpenMetadata outputs into a location python-cheatsheet reads, then leakage becomes possible.
mitigations: Keep OpenMetadata outputs out of shared folders.
Avoid pasting metadata into python-cheatsheet docs.
Review OpenMetadata exports for sensitive lineage or governance fields.
Use separate accounts and workspaces for the two agents.
requires-engineering: enforce access controls on any shared export location.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenMetadata supports multiple instances and can write through APIs, SDKs, events, webhooks, and MCP, but python-cheatsheet is documentation-only with no write, network, or subprocess capability. Because only one side can mutate state, there is no meaningful concurrent write conflict in the default pair; uncertainty is low and the blast radius is small.
conditions: IF python-cheatsheet is replaced with a writable agent, then overlapping writes could conflict.
IF OpenMetadata is pointed at a shared mutable backend with another writer, then coordination issues can arise.
mitigations: Keep python-cheatsheet read-only.
Avoid connecting OpenMetadata to shared mutable resources without locks.
Schedule OpenMetadata writes outside any manual editing window.
Use separate repositories or databases for mutable outputs.
requires-engineering: add optimistic locking on shared backends.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenMetadata can produce metadata and governance outputs, but python-cheatsheet is documentation-only and has no action-taking authority such as email, shell, or network egress. That makes a harmful cascade unlikely by default; at most, python-cheatsheet could misrender OpenMetadata content if a human manually transfers it.
conditions: IF a human treats OpenMetadata output as authoritative and republishes it in python-cheatsheet without verification, then errors can cascade.
IF python-cheatsheet is embedded into a downstream automation layer, then its text could influence actions.
mitigations: Verify OpenMetadata outputs before reuse.
Mark python-cheatsheet content as non-authoritative reference material.
Do not automate actions from python-cheatsheet text.
Add a review checklist for copied metadata.
requires-engineering: add validation against source-of-truth records.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenMetadata touches governance and memory/tribal knowledge, which can include regulated or sensitive metadata, while python-cheatsheet is documentation-only and touches no declared data classes. The pair does not show a residency or certification mismatch directly, but any compliance issue would arise if sensitive OpenMetadata exports are manually placed into the documentation artifact.
conditions: IF regulated metadata from OpenMetadata is copied into python-cheatsheet, then retention and access controls may diverge.
IF the documentation repository has a different residency or retention policy than the OpenMetadata deployment, then compliance mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Exclude regulated fields from copied examples.
Review documentation retention settings.
Keep OpenMetadata and python-cheatsheet under separate policy domains.
Add a short compliance checklist before publishing docs.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based redaction on exports.
